book.p: 1 The Judaeo-Arabic text appears to be corrupt here. The original may have read: …an yaʿtaqida anna -llāha l-ʿālim bi-asrihi. The Arabic version may reflect an emendation of the corrupt text. Our translation reflects the tentative emendation. Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 148: “that He possesses the total universe, the heavens and what is in them…”

1 This may be a reference to Exodus 15:26, in which God promises to protect the Israelites from the diseases (ha-maḥalah) inflicted upon the Israelites, although the Arabic is ambiguous. Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 150 n. 18.

1 The term qibla means “direction” and refers to the direction properly faced during prayer (and, according to our author, other devotional acts). There is no accurate English translation that comfortably fits this context.

1 This translation follows our edition, based on MSS JTSb and BL, which read al-mīʿād (from the root w-ʿ-d). JTSa and BLb read al-maʿād (the Return; from the root ʿ-w-d). Both expressions are widely attested in medieval Arabic literature across schools and genres.

2 The sense here seems to be that divine judgment takes into account the full range of hidden merit and guilt; according to this reading, connecting the lexeme to the following phrase, it could be read khāfiya. So reads the Arabic version. Alternatively, one could connect the term to the preceding phrase: jumlatan kāfiyatan, “altogether, sufficiently (i.e., fully).” Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 153: “entirely and summarily.” The two possible readings rest on a single diacritic, which is rarely provided in the MSS.

1 In its Biblical context, “eternal God” would be a better translation. Our translation of al-Maghribī's usage here more closely reflects Maimonides' understanding of this verse. The latter's usage of this citation as a preface for his works echoes the Islamic basmala (pace Joseph Qafiḥ, for whose discussion see Moreh ha-nebukhim [Mossad Harav Kook: 1977], 3 n. 4). Qafiḥ notes that in employing this formulation, Maimonides expresses his identification with Abraham, the messenger of monotheism in an idolatrous world. In the period following Maimonides, this became a very standard opening in medieval Hebrew and Judaeo-Arabic works. For Maimonides' usage and interpretation of this verse, see Guide of the Perplexed (trans. Shlomo Pines; Chicago: 1963), 3 and n. 1 (introductory epistle), 282 and n. 4 (II.13), 516 (III.29); and cf. Mishneh Torah, Laws of Idolatry and Gentile Norms, 1:3. Saul Lieberman noted that Maimonides prefaces all of his works with this formulation (see Hilkhoth Ha-Yerushalmi (The Laws of the Palestinian Talmud) of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, ed. Saul Lieberman [The Jewish Theological Seminary of America: 1995], 5, n. 7). Of course, the fact that Maimonides' usage of Gen. 21:33 echoes the basmala does not in the least negate Qafiḥ's insightful observation concerning the significance of this usage.
1 The term baṣīr may denote either mental insight or physical sight.
1 It seems that the version attested in JTSb and BLb reflects an erroneous reading of thikhan (without diacritic: תכן) as takūn (תכון).

1 Despite the fact that JTSb presents the more difficult reading (lectio difficilior) and appears to be older, we have based our text and translation on the version that appears in BL and BLb. The reading sāʾiran wa-jāʾi (sic) is more plausible on two grounds: The formulation is used elsewhere by the same author (see the second tenet of al-Maghribī's creed); and it is arguably cognate with the rabbinic terms holakhah and habaʾah, for which cf. Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Ritual Slaughter, 3:11. This Hebrew terminology is also reflected in Hebrew Karaite works, both medieval and modern: Cf. the formulations ve-yolikh ve-yavi ʿad she-yashlim ha-sheḥiṭah and ve-yolikh ve-yavi ha-sakkin in the eighth chapter of the Hebrew version of al-Maghribī's monograph; Aaron b. Elijah of Nicomedia (fourteenth century), Gan ʿEden, ed. Judah b. Isaac Savuskan (Gözlöw [Eupatoria]: 1864), Ritual Slaughter, 89; and Shemuel Ha-kohen, ʿInyan ha-sheḥiṭah/Ritual Slaughter: A Modern Guide to Karaite Jewish Practice (The Karaite Jews of America: 2017 [republished from 1958 edition]), 18. Cf. Nemoy, “Israel Al-Maghribī's Tract,” 200: “back and forth.” (Nemoy follows the modern Arabic version.)

1 Reading the Judaeo-Arabic jāra with the Arabic version as jarra, and understanding the term כ̇נק as a variant of the makhnaq (throat). Although ʿunq (as in the Arabic version) is a more common term, (a) the Judaeo-Arabic provides the lectio difficilior, and (b) the term ʿunq refers either to the neck as a whole or to the nape or back of the neck, which makes less sense in this context.

1 The Judaeo-Arabic version attested in JTSb and BL appears to be corrupt here, due to a series of scribal errors and emendations (apparently wṣyd > wṣyr > yṣyr > wyṣyr [wa-yaṣīr]; both yod/vav and dalet/resh are easily confused in Hebrew script). Our edition and translation follow BLb and the Arabic-script version, providing the variants in the critical apparatus.

2 The Judaeo-Arabic text in JTSb and BL is corrupt here and difficult to decipher. On purely textual grounds, our text follows JTSb and BL, presenting as they do the lectio difficilior. Our translation follows BLb, despite the fact that it presents the lectio facilior, as it is at least decipherable.
1 Compare Targum Onqelos, and Ibn Ezra's interpretation ad loc.; this also reflects al-Maghribī's interpretation of shehiyyah as a response to being startled.
2 Compare Ibn Ezra's commentary ad loc., where he explains לא גרמו as לא שברו עצם (cf. Aramaic g-r-m as “bone”).
3 Apparently identifying the root ḥ-l-d as a metathesis of ḥ-d-l; compare Ibn Ezra ad loc.

1 All of the Judaeo-Arabic manuscripts available to us seem to read ʿadiya. The text appears to be corrupt, possibly reflecting a scribal error ʿariya > ʿadiya. The Arabic version (ʿudda), apart from remaining difficult to understand, seems to reflect an interpretation of the latter reading. The translation follows the suggested emendation.
1 This section bears no title in the original Judaeo-Arabic; we have added one to assist the reader's transition to this new topic. Please note that our translations of animal anatomy are tentative.

2 The Judaeo-Arabic version appears to be corrupt here. JTSb, BLb, and the Arabic version have מכ̇צה / مخصة without a diacritic over the ṣād, while BL reads מכ̇צ̇ה. (It should be noted, however, that BLb is extremely inconsistent in applying diacritics, even in cases where this is common in Judaeo-Arabic MSS, e.g., to indicate ḍād and ẓāʾ.) The former reading makes little sense, and the most plausible (though still awkward, and certainly speculative) emendation would have מכ̇צצה̈. If BL does not reflect the original version, the copyist of BL (or the copyist of the vorlage) may have emended the ṣād to a ḍād in an attempt to read the lexeme as a specific anatomical term, derived from the root m-kh-ḍ (to shake or churn [e.g., milk]). This could plausibly refer to the mammary artery.
